note:
The patient is a 23-year-old male seen in the dermatology clinic for follow-up of acne vulgaris that began in his mid-teens. He reports inflammatory papules and pustules across the cheeks, forehead, and jawline, with occasional painful nodules along the left jawline that leave dark marks when they resolve. Over the past 6 months he has used an over-the-counter benzoyl peroxide 5% wash once daily with only partial improvement. He denies itching or burning of the skin, denies fever, and denies any previous prescription acne treatment. He has no other medical conditions, takes no other medications, and has no known drug allergies. He is a university student, does not smoke, and has not noticed worsening with particular foods.

On examination he is well appearing. There are scattered inflammatory papules and pustules across both cheeks and the forehead, comedones on the nose and chin, and three tender nodules along the left jawline. There is mild post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation but no ice-pick scarring, and the chest and back are clear.

My impression is moderate inflammatory acne vulgaris with a partial response to benzoyl peroxide alone. I am starting tretinoin 0.025% cream, to be applied to the face every night at bedtime, and he will continue the benzoyl peroxide wash each morning. I counseled him on sun protection, using a non-comedogenic moisturizer, and the expected early dryness and irritation. He will return in 12 weeks to reassess his response, and we will discuss other options at that visit if improvement is inadequate.
summary: A 23-year-old male was seen in dermatology clinic for follow-up of acne vulgaris present since his mid-teens, with only partial improvement from an over-the-counter benzoyl peroxide wash. He has inflammatory papules, pustules and tender nodules, and denies itching, burning, and fever. Examination showed scattered inflammatory lesions on the face, comedones, mild post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, no ice-pick scarring, and a clear chest and back. The impression is moderate inflammatory acne vulgaris. Tretinoin 0.025% cream is started at bedtime alongside continued benzoyl peroxide, with sun protection counseling and a return visit in 12 weeks.

note: Dictation for a 21-year-old female seen in the ear, nose, and throat clinic for recurrent tonsillitis. Her mother accompanies her and provides part of the history. The patient reports repeated sore throats with painful swallowing, and her mother says she has had five episodes in the past year, correction, six episodes in the past year, each lasting about one week and each treated by her primary care doctor with a course of antibiotics. The most recent episode ended three weeks ago. She has missed several days of work because of fever and throat pain. Between episodes she notices bad breath and occasional tonsil stones. She denies ear pain, denies difficulty breathing, and denies loud snoring or witnessed pauses in breathing at night. Her mother also asks whether the eye redness she had during one of the infections was related, and the patient says there was no eye pain and no change in her vision. She has no other medical conditions, takes only an oral contraceptive pill, and has no known drug allergies. On exam today she is afebrile and comfortable. The tonsils are enlarged, two plus bilaterally, with a small amount of white debris in the crypts and no exudate or asymmetry. There is a tender right anterior cervical node about one centimeter in size. The ears and nose are normal, and the eyes show no conjunctival injection with normal lids. Impression is recurrent tonsillitis with a significant effect on work, and I think she is a good candidate for tonsillectomy. I discussed the procedure including the risks of bleeding and pain after surgery, which the patient and her mother understand. I will order preoperative blood work today, no antibiotics are needed today, and she will return to clinic in four weeks to schedule surgery.
summary: A 21-year-old female attended with her mother for recurrent tonsillitis, with six episodes of sore throat and painful swallowing in the past year, each treated with antibiotics. She has missed work because of fever and throat pain and denies ear pain, breathing difficulty, snoring, eye pain, and vision change. Examination showed enlarged tonsils with white debris in the crypts and a tender right anterior cervical node. The impression is recurrent tonsillitis with a significant effect on work, making her a good candidate for tonsillectomy. Plan is preoperative blood work, no antibiotics today, and return in four weeks to schedule surgery.

note:
Doctor: Good morning. I understand you are a 96-year-old female and you have been having some trouble with your memory?
Patient: Yes, that's right. I keep misplacing my glasses, and sometimes I forget what I went into a room for.
Doctor: How long has this been going on?
Patient: Oh, maybe a year or so. It has gotten a little worse lately.
Doctor: Do you get lost when you are out, or have trouble paying bills and taking your medicines?
Patient: No, I don't get lost. I still pay my bills myself, and I use a pill box for my medicine.
Doctor: Any falls, any confusion at night, or any hallucinations?
Patient: No falls, no confusion at night, and I don't see things that aren't there.
Doctor: How are your mood and sleep?
Patient: My mood is fine and I sleep well enough.
Doctor: What medicines do you take?
Patient: Amlodipine 5 mg once a day for my high blood pressure, and a vitamin D tablet.
Doctor: Good. Today your blood pressure is 134/72 and your heart rate is 68. You are alert and pleasant, and you walked into the room steadily without help. On the Montreal Cognitive Assessment you scored 22 out of 30, mostly losing points on delayed recall.
Patient: Is that bad?
Doctor: It fits with mild cognitive impairment, which is more than normal forgetfulness but not dementia, because you are still managing your daily tasks on your own. I'm going to check a vitamin B12 level and a TSH today to rule out simple causes. I don't recommend starting a memory medication right now.
Patient: That sounds fine to me.
Doctor: Please keep using your pill box and stay active. We will see you back in six months to repeat the testing.
summary: A 96-year-old female presented with about a year of memory trouble, including misplacing her glasses and forgetting why she entered a room, slightly worse lately. She still pays her own bills and uses a pill box, and she denies falls, confusion at night, and hallucinations. Blood pressure was 134/72, and she scored 22 out of 30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, losing points mostly on delayed recall. The impression is mild cognitive impairment. A vitamin B12 level and TSH are ordered, no memory medication is started, and she will return in six months to repeat the testing.

soap.assessment: Mild cognitive impairment, with daily tasks still managed independently. High blood pressure.

note: Dictating a nephrology clinic follow-up for a 40-year-old male with chronic kidney disease stage 3b attributed to long-standing hypertension. He missed his last appointment because he has no reliable car and lives about ninety minutes from the clinic, and the bus to our area runs only a few times a day. He reports mild fatigue but denies swelling of the legs, denies foamy urine, denies decreased urine output, and denies nausea or vomiting. He takes lisinopril 20 mg once daily and has no known drug allergies. He avoids anti-inflammatory pain relievers and does not smoke. Blood pressure today is 138 over 84, heart rate 74, and weight is stable. On exam there is no peripheral edema, the lungs are clear, and the heart sounds are regular. Labs drawn today show creatinine 2.2 mg/dL with an eGFR of 38, potassium 4.7, bicarbonate 22, and a urine albumin to creatinine ratio of 210 mg/g. Compared with six months ago his kidney function is unchanged. Impression is chronic kidney disease stage 3b, stable, with moderately increased albuminuria and blood pressure slightly above goal. Plan is to increase lisinopril to 40 mg once daily. Because travel is difficult, he will have a basic metabolic panel drawn at a laboratory near his home two weeks after the dose change, and I will review the result by phone. I am placing a social work referral for transportation assistance. His next visit in three months will be by video, with an in-person visit in six months. I also reinforced avoiding NSAIDs.

Lisinopril is increased to 40 mg once daily, labs will be drawn near his home, and a social work referral and video follow-up are arranged.

note:
Telehealth video visit for endocrinology follow-up. The patient is a 61-year-old male with T1DM on an insulin pump and a continuous glucose monitor, connecting from home by video with good audio and picture. His identity was confirmed and he agreed to a video visit.

He reports frequent low glucose readings over the past month, mostly between 2 and 4 AM and again in the mid-afternoon after his walks. He feels shaky and sweaty with the lows and treats them with glucose tablets. He denies passing out, denies seizures, and denies ever needing glucagon or emergency help. He also denies chest pain and palpitations. He still feels the warning symptoms before a low. Current pump settings use insulin aspart with an overnight basal rate of 0.9 units per hour and a lunch insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio of 1 to 8. He also has HTN and hyperlipidemia, for which he takes lisinopril 10 mg once daily and atorvastatin 20 mg nightly. He has no known drug allergies.

Home readings today are BP 126/74, heart rate 66, and weight 84 kg. The CGM report shared through the clinic portal shows time in range 71%, time below 70 mg/dL at 9%, and time below 54 mg/dL at 3%, with an average glucose of 138 mg/dL. His A1c from last week's lab was 6.4%. On video he looks well, speaks in full sentences, has no tremor, and the infusion site on his abdomen looks clean without redness. No hands-on exam was possible.

My impression is T1DM with recurrent hypoglycemia, mostly overnight and after exercise, driven by basal and carbohydrate ratio settings that are too aggressive. His HTN and hyperlipidemia are stable on current medications.

I am reducing the overnight basal rate from 0.9 units per hour to 0.75 units per hour and changing the lunch insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio from 1 to 8 to 1 to 10. I am also raising the CGM low alert from 70 to 80 mg/dL. I am prescribing nasal glucagon 3 mg to keep at home, to be used as needed for severe lows, and I reviewed how to use it with him. He should eat 15 to 20 grams of carbohydrate before his afternoon walks. Continue lisinopril and atorvastatin unchanged. He will upload his CGM data in two weeks for review, repeat the A1c and a lipid panel in three months, and return for a video visit in six weeks.

Home blood pressure was 126/74, CGM time below 70 mg/dL was 9%, and A1c was 6.4%, and he looked well on video. The impression is T1DM with recurrent hypoglycemia from overly aggressive basal and carbohydrate ratio settings, with HTN and hyperlipidemia stable. The overnight basal rate and lunch carbohydrate ratio are reduced, the CGM low alert is raised, nasal glucagon 3 mg is prescribed, and a video visit is planned in six weeks.

note: Psychiatry evaluation dictation on the hospital ward for a 20-year-old male who is medically cleared after an overnight observation stay for dehydration and was referred by the primary team for an adult ADHD evaluation. He is a college student who reports trouble sustaining attention since grade school, with teacher comments about daydreaming, careless mistakes, and not finishing work. He now loses track of assignments, loses his keys and phone, becomes distracted within minutes of starting to read, and feels restless and fidgety during lectures. His grades have dropped this year and he is at risk of academic probation. His mother, correction, his father, who is at the bedside, confirms the symptoms were present before age twelve. He denies depressed mood, denies decreased need for sleep or periods of elevated mood, denies hallucinations, and denies thoughts of harming himself. He denies alcohol and drug use. He takes no regular medications and has no known drug allergies. He has no known heart problems and no family history of sudden cardiac death. Blood pressure is 118/72 and heart rate is 70. On mental status exam he is calm and cooperative, speech is normal, mood is described as fine, affect is full, thought process is linear, and there is no psychosis. His Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale screener is positive with 5 of 6 items. Impression is ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation. Plan is to start methylphenidate extended release 18 mg every morning, with titration at follow-up. He has no car and the campus is far from our clinic, so follow-up will be a video visit in two weeks and I will send the prescription to a pharmacy near campus. Social work will arrange transportation vouchers. Return precautions for chest pain, palpitations, or poor sleep were reviewed with him.

His father confirms the symptoms were present before age twelve, and he denies depressed mood, elevated mood, hallucinations, and thoughts of self-harm. The Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale screener was positive, with normal vital signs and mental status. The impression is ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation. Methylphenidate extended release 18 mg every morning is started, with video follow-up in two weeks, a prescription sent near campus, and social work help for transportation.

note:
13-year-old male, outpatient peds clinic, here w/ mother for sore throat
CC: sore throat x 3d + fever
HPI: sore throat x3d, worse w/ swallowing. Fever to 39 C at home yesterday. HA, mild abd pain. No cough, no rhinorrhea, no hoarseness. No vomiting, denies rash. Denies drooling or trouble swallowing saliva. No neck stiffness. No known strep contacts but brother at same school w/ ST last wk.
PMH: allergic rhinitis, on cetirizine 10 mg daily, well controlled. Otherwise healthy. Immunizations UTD.
Allergy: penicillin - hives after amoxicillin at age 5y, mother confirms. No other drug allergies.
Meds: cetirizine 10 mg daily. Took acetaminophen 500 mg x1 this AM w/ some relief.
SH: 8th grade, lives w/ parents, no smokers at home.

Vitals: Temp 38.6 C, HR 102, RR 18, BP 112/68, SpO2 99% RA, wt 52 kg
PE: NAD, nontoxic. Tonsils 3+ bilat w/ erythema + white exudates, palatal petechiae. Uvula midline, no trismus, no peritonsillar bulge. Tender anterior cervical LAD bilat. No scarlatiniform rash. TMs clear. Lungs CTAB. Abd soft NT, no HSM.
Rapid strep test: POSITIVE

Dx: strep pharyngitis (RADT +)
Allergic rhinitis - stable
Penicillin allergy - hives, so avoiding penicillins and using non-beta-lactam abx

Rx/plan:
- Start clindamycin 300 mg PO TID x10d (about 17 mg/kg/day). Take w/ full glass of water.
- Acetaminophen 650 mg q6h PRN pain/fever, max 4 doses/day.
- Cont cetirizine 10 mg daily.
- Salt water gargles, cold fluids, rest.
- Stay home from school until 24h on abx + afebrile.
- Counseled on diarrhea w/ clindamycin: stop and call if severe or bloody diarrhea.
- Return/ED if drooling, trouble breathing, neck stiffness, rash, or persistent fever >48h after starting abx.
- Refer to allergy for penicillin allergy testing, non-urgent.
- F/u PRN, or in 3d if not improving. Mother voiced understanding.
summary: A 13-year-old male presented with his mother for 3 days of sore throat and fever, with headache and mild abdominal pain but no cough, rhinorrhea, hoarseness, vomiting, or rash. He has allergic rhinitis on cetirizine and a documented penicillin allergy with hives after amoxicillin at age 5. He was febrile at 38.6 C with large erythematous tonsils with white exudates, palatal petechiae, and tender anterior cervical nodes, and the rapid strep test was positive. The diagnosis is strep pharyngitis. Because of the penicillin allergy, clindamycin 300 mg three times daily for 10 days is started along with acetaminophen, and allergy referral is arranged.

soap.subjective: 13-year-old male with 3 days of sore throat worse with swallowing and fever to 39 C at home, plus headache and mild abdominal pain. No cough, rhinorrhea, hoarseness, vomiting, rash, drooling, trouble swallowing saliva, or neck stiffness. Brother at the same school had a sore throat last week. Allergic rhinitis on cetirizine 10 mg daily. Allergic to penicillin with hives after amoxicillin at age 5. Took acetaminophen 500 mg this morning with some relief.
soap.objective: Temp 38.6 C, HR 102, RR 18, BP 112/68, SpO2 99% on room air, weight 52 kg. No acute distress and nontoxic. Tonsils 3+ bilaterally with erythema and white exudates, palatal petechiae, midline uvula, no trismus or peritonsillar bulge. Tender bilateral anterior cervical adenopathy, no scarlatiniform rash. TMs clear, lungs clear, abdomen soft and nontender without hepatosplenomegaly. Rapid strep test positive.
soap.assessment: Strep pharyngitis confirmed by rapid test. Allergic rhinitis, stable. Penicillin allergy with hives, requiring a non-beta-lactam antibiotic.
plan: Start clindamycin 300 mg PO three times daily for 10 days, taken with a full glass of water
Acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain or fever, maximum 4 doses per day
Continue cetirizine 10 mg daily
Salt water gargles, cold fluids, and rest
Stay home from school until 24 hours on antibiotics and afebrile
Counseled to stop clindamycin and call if severe or bloody diarrhea develops
Return or go to the ED for drooling, trouble breathing, neck stiffness, rash, or persistent fever more than 48 hours after starting antibiotics
Non-urgent allergy referral for penicillin allergy testing
Follow up as needed, or in 3 days if not improving

note:
Doctor: Hello, I see you are a 66-year-old male and you came in today because you think you might have ADHD?
Patient: Yes. I just got back from a two-week trip overseas, and it was a mess. I nearly missed two flights, lost my passport, and left my phone in a taxi. My wife says that is how I have always been, and my grandson was just diagnosed with ADHD, so I started wondering.
Doctor: Tell me about it. When did the trouble with focus start?
Patient: Since I was a kid. I could never sit still in class, I zone out in conversations, I lose things all the time, and I start projects and never finish them.
Doctor: Has it caused trouble at work?
Patient: I'm retired now, but it cost me a couple of jobs.
Doctor: Any low mood, anxiety, trouble sleeping, or heavy alcohol use?
Patient: No, my mood is fine, I sleep okay, and I only have a beer on weekends.
Doctor: Since you just traveled, any fever, diarrhea, or cough?
Patient: No fever, no diarrhea, and no cough. I feel fine.
Doctor: Any chest pain or palpitations?
Patient: None. I take lisinopril 10 mg once a day for high blood pressure, and that is all.
Doctor: Your blood pressure today is 138/82 and your heart rate is 76. You are alert and engaged, your heart sounds normal, and your lungs are clear. The ASRS screening questionnaire you filled out was positive. Based on your history, this could be ADHD, but urgent care is not the right place to make that diagnosis or to start a stimulant.
Patient: So what do I do?
Doctor: I am referring you to outpatient psychiatry for a full ADHD evaluation, and I would like your primary doctor to do an ECG before any stimulant is considered. I am not starting any new medicine today. Keep taking your lisinopril, and come back or go to the emergency room if you develop fever, diarrhea, or chest pain.
Patient: That sounds reasonable. Thank you.
summary: A 66-year-old male presented to urgent care wondering about ADHD after a two-week overseas trip during which he nearly missed flights and lost his passport and phone. He reports lifelong inattention, restlessness in class, zoning out in conversations, losing things, and unfinished projects that cost him some jobs. He denies low mood, fever, diarrhea, cough, chest pain, and palpitations, and takes lisinopril for high blood pressure. Vitals were normal and the ASRS screening questionnaire was positive. The working impression is possible ADHD, with outpatient psychiatry referral, an ECG through his primary doctor, and no new medication started.

soap.assessment: Possible ADHD based on history and a positive screen; formal diagnosis and stimulant treatment not appropriate in urgent care. High blood pressure.

Return or go to the emergency room for fever, diarrhea, or chest pain

note:
Nurse: Triage note for the doctor. This is a 33-year-old female with lung cancer on immunotherapy, here with cough and shortness of breath. Oxygen saturation is 92% on room air and temperature is 37.8 Celsius.
Doctor: Thank you. Hello, I'm sorry you are not feeling well. I see you are a 33-year-old female with stage four lung adenocarcinoma. What has been going on?
Patient: I've had a dry cough for about five days, and over the last two days I get winded just walking up the stairs. That is not normal for me.
Doctor: Any fever or chills?
Patient: I felt warm last night and my thermometer said 99.9, but no shaking chills.
Doctor: Any chest pain, or coughing up blood?
Patient: No chest pain and no blood.
Doctor: Any leg pain or swelling?
Patient: No, my legs feel fine.
Doctor: I understand you recently traveled.
Patient: Yes, I got back eight days ago from a family wedding in Portugal. The flights were about ten hours each way.
Doctor: Any diarrhea, vomiting, or rash while you were away or since?
Patient: No diarrhea, no vomiting, and no rash. My cousin had a cold at the wedding, though.
Doctor: Okay. Tell me about your medicines.
Patient: I get pembrolizumab 200 mg by IV every three weeks, and my last infusion was ten days ago. I take levothyroxine 100 micrograms every morning for the underactive thyroid the immunotherapy caused. Wait, sorry, that is wrong. My endocrinologist lowered it to 75 micrograms four weeks ago, so it is 75.
Doctor: So levothyroxine 75 micrograms every morning, not 100. Is that right?
Patient: Yes, 75. I also have asthma, so I use albuterol, 2 puffs as needed, and I have needed it three or four times a day this week. I was on omeprazole 20 mg once a day for reflux, but I stopped it two weeks ago because my reflux got better. I have been taking ibuprofen 400 mg for headaches a few times this week, and acetaminophen 650 mg sometimes.
Doctor: Any drug allergies?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Thank you. Now your exam. Your heart rate is 108, respiratory rate 22, blood pressure 112/70, and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. You look tired but you are speaking in full sentences. I hear fine crackles at the bottom of both lungs with no wheezing. Your heart is fast but regular. Your calves are not swollen or tender, and both legs look the same. Your belly is soft and there is no rash.
Patient: What do the tests show?
Doctor: The chest x-ray shows hazy patchy opacities in both lower lungs, with no large effusion and no collapsed lung. The rapid COVID and flu tests are both negative. Your white blood cell count is 9.8, hemoglobin is 11.4, and creatinine is 0.7. The D-dimer is elevated at 1.9, which is nonspecific in someone with cancer. Your urine pregnancy test is negative. We gave you oxygen at 2 liters per minute and your saturation is up to 95%.
Patient: What do you think this is?
Doctor: The most likely explanation is pneumonitis, which is inflammation of the lungs caused by your immunotherapy. A lung infection and a blood clot in the lungs are also possible after your long flights, and your oxygen is low, so I cannot safely sort this out here. I am sending you by ambulance to the emergency department for a CT angiogram of the chest and further workup. I am calling the oncologist on call myself. Please do not receive your next pembrolizumab dose until oncology reviews you. I am not starting steroids here, because the emergency team and oncology will decide that after the CT. Stop the ibuprofen and use acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours as needed instead. note:
Hospital day 3 progress note for an 85-year-old male admitted with an acute gout flare of the right ankle. He presented with two days of severe right ankle pain, swelling, and warmth and could not bear weight. Arthrocentesis of the right ankle on admission returned cloudy fluid with a white cell count of 28,000, needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals, a negative Gram stain, and cultures with no growth to date. He has a history of gout, chronic kidney disease stage 3b, and hypertension. Before admission he took allopurinol 100 mg daily and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, and he had been taking colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily for 2 days, which caused loose stools and did not help.

Overnight he was afebrile and slept fairly well. This morning he reports that his ankle pain has improved from 8 out of 10 to 4 out of 10 since starting prednisone. He denies fever, chills, chest pain, and pain in any other joint. The loose stools have resolved since colchicine was stopped.

Vitals this morning are temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 76, blood pressure 148/84, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. The right ankle remains swollen and warm with mild erythema and tenderness over the lateral malleolus, and range of motion is limited, but he can bear partial weight with a walker. The other joints are without swelling. His heart is regular, lungs are clear, and there is no edema of the legs.

Uric acid was 9.6 mg/dL on admission. Creatinine is 1.7 mg/dL with an eGFR of 38, unchanged from admission, the white blood cell count has fallen from 13.2 to 11.4, and C-reactive protein has fallen from 62 to 34 mg/L. The right ankle x-ray showed soft tissue swelling without fracture or erosions.

My assessment is an acute gout flare of the right ankle that is improving on prednisone. His chronic kidney disease limits the use of colchicine and anti-inflammatory drugs, and the hydrochlorothiazide likely contributed to the flare. His blood pressure is above goal.

For the plan, continue prednisone 30 mg once daily and taper over 10 days after discharge. Colchicine remains stopped. Stop hydrochlorothiazide and start amlodipine 5 mg daily for blood pressure. Continue allopurinol 100 mg daily and recheck a uric acid level in four weeks with the goal of titrating the dose. Avoid NSAIDs. Ice and elevate the ankle, and ask physical therapy to evaluate him for a walker before discharge. Discharge is anticipated in one to two days if his pain keeps improving, with rheumatology follow-up in four weeks.

Telehealth note for a telephone visit only, with no video. The patient is a 71-year-old male with chronic rhinosinusitis, seen by phone from his home for follow-up of ongoing sinus symptoms. His identity was verified with two identifiers and he agreed to a phone visit.

He reports nasal congestion, thick yellow-green drainage down the back of his throat, pressure over both cheeks and between the eyes, and a reduced sense of smell for more than three months, worse over the last three weeks. He has been using oxymetazoline nasal spray twice a day for the past three weeks and says it helps for only a few hours before the stuffiness returns. He also has fluticasone nasal spray, 2 sprays in each nostril once daily, but uses it only about half the time. He has not been doing saline rinses. He denies fever, denies facial swelling, denies eye pain or redness, denies double vision or any change in his vision, and denies nosebleeds. He has hypertension and takes lisinopril 10 mg once daily. He has no known drug allergies.

He has a home blood pressure cuff, and his blood pressure today is 134/80 with a pulse of 72. A CT of the sinuses done last month showed mucosal thickening in both maxillary and ethmoid sinuses with no polyps and no bony erosion. No physical exam or nasal endoscopy was possible by phone. He spoke in full sentences throughout the call and sounded congested, without cough or hoarseness.

Impression is chronic rhinosinusitis with an acute flare of purulent drainage, and probable rebound congestion from prolonged use of oxymetazoline. His hypertension appears controlled on his current treatment.

I am stopping the oxymetazoline today, because use beyond three days can make congestion worse. I am starting doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days, to be taken with food and a full glass of water, with sun protection. He should use the fluticasone nasal spray, 2 sprays in each nostril once daily, every day, and start saline rinses with distilled water twice daily. He will continue lisinopril. He should seek urgent care for swelling around the eyes, vision changes, severe headache, or high fever. I am scheduling an in-person visit in three weeks for nasal endoscopy, and we will discuss referral for sinus surgery if symptoms persist.

Because her symptoms bother her a great deal, I am also starting mirabegron 25 mg once daily. I explained that it can raise blood pressure, so she will keep checking it at home. She will also start pelvic floor exercises. Follow-up will be by video in six weeks to review the bladder diary and her response to treatment.

The patient is a 79-year-old female seen in the cardiology clinic for evaluation of palpitations. She describes episodes of rapid, irregular heartbeats over the past two months, lasting from a few minutes up to a few hours, sometimes with mild lightheadedness. The episodes occur at rest, mostly in the evening. She denies chest pain, fainting, shortness of breath, and leg swelling. Because she takes an anticoagulant, I asked about bleeding, and she denies black stools, blood in the urine, nosebleeds, and easy bruising. Her caffeine intake is one cup of tea in the morning.

Her history includes paroxysmal atrial fibrillation diagnosed last year, hypertension, and hypothyroidism. Current medications are apixaban 5 mg twice daily, metoprolol succinate 25 mg once daily, and levothyroxine 75 mcg once daily. She has no known drug allergies and says she has not missed any doses of apixaban.

In clinic her blood pressure is 128/74, her pulse is 68, and her weight is 66 kg. She appears comfortable. There is no jugular venous distension, the heart rhythm is regular with occasional extra beats and no murmurs, the lungs are clear, and the legs show no edema or bruising. An ECG today shows sinus rhythm at 66 beats per minute with occasional premature atrial contractions. A 14-day patch monitor completed last week showed paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with a burden of 9 percent, the longest episode lasting 3 hours and 40 minutes with ventricular rates up to 128, and her symptoms matched these episodes. There were no pauses and no ventricular tachycardia. An echocardiogram last year showed an ejection fraction of 60 percent with mild left atrial enlargement. Her TSH last month was 1.9, creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL, and hemoglobin is 12.8 g/dL.

My impression is symptomatic paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular rates during episodes. She remains appropriately anticoagulated, and her apixaban dose is correct for her age, weight, and creatinine. Her hypertension and hypothyroidism are stable.

I am increasing metoprolol succinate from 25 mg to 50 mg once daily to slow the rate during episodes. She will continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily and levothyroxine unchanged. I reviewed bleeding precautions and advised her to avoid NSAIDs. We will check a basic metabolic panel and a CBC in two weeks, and she will return in three months. If symptoms persist on the higher beta blocker dose, we will discuss rhythm control options. She should go to the emergency department for fainting, chest pain, or any bleeding that does not stop.

The patient is a 28-year-old female, gravida 2 para 1, at 34 weeks of gestation, seen in the obstetrics clinic for evaluation of possible preeclampsia after an elevated blood pressure at a routine visit earlier this week. She reports a mild frontal headache for the past two days and new swelling of her feet. She denies blurred vision, spots in her vision, right upper abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting, shortness of breath, vaginal bleeding, and leakage of fluid. She reports good fetal movement. Her pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated, and her blood pressures at all earlier visits were normal. She takes a prenatal vitamin daily and aspirin 81 mg daily, which she started at 12 weeks, and she has taken ibuprofen 400 mg a few times this week for the headaches. She has no known drug allergies.

On exam her blood pressure is 148/94, and after 15 minutes of rest the repeat is 144/92. Heart rate is 84 and temperature is normal. She appears comfortable. She has 1+ pitting edema of both feet and ankles. Reflexes are normal without clonus, and there is no right upper quadrant tenderness. Fundal height is 34 cm and the fetal heart rate is 142 beats per minute. Urine dipstick shows 1+ protein. The urine protein to creatinine ratio is 0.42. Platelets are 198, creatinine is 0.7 mg/dL, AST is 26, and ALT is 21. A non-stress test was reactive. Ultrasound shows an estimated fetal weight at the 45th percentile and a normal amniotic fluid index.

My impression is preeclampsia without severe features at 34 weeks. Her blood pressures are below 160/110, her labs are normal, and her symptoms are mild, so she can be managed as an outpatient with close surveillance.

I am starting labetalol 100 mg twice daily. I asked her to stop ibuprofen and use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for headaches instead, and to continue aspirin 81 mg daily and the prenatal vitamin. She will check her blood pressure at home twice a day and keep a log. We will repeat the labs weekly and repeat the non-stress test twice weekly, with a growth ultrasound in two weeks. Delivery is planned at 37 weeks, or sooner if severe features develop. I reviewed warning signs, and she should go to labor and delivery triage right away for severe headache, vision changes, upper abdominal pain, shortness of breath, a blood pressure of 160/110 or higher, or decreased fetal movement. Follow-up in the clinic in three days.

The patient is a 25-year-old female seen in the dermatology clinic for a flare of atopic dermatitis that began about six weeks ago. She is visibly anxious and asked many questions throughout the visit, including whether the condition is contagious, whether topical steroids will thin her skin permanently, whether diet is causing it, and whether she will need injections for the rest of her life. I answered each question in turn, and she said she felt more reassured by the end of the visit.

She has had eczema since childhood. The current flare involves itchy, dry, red patches in the folds of both elbows, behind the knees, and on the sides of her neck, with itch that wakes her from sleep several nights a week. She denies fever, denies oozing or crusting, and denies new soaps, detergents, or pets. She has seasonal allergic rhinitis and takes cetirizine 10 mg once daily. She has been applying over-the-counter hydrocortisone 1% cream once or twice a day with little benefit, and she moisturizes only occasionally. She has no known drug allergies.

Her office blood pressure is 110/68 and heart rate is 74. Exam shows lichenified erythematous plaques in both antecubital fossae and both popliteal fossae, with excoriations and mild scale on the sides of the neck, and dry skin on the forearms. There is no weeping, no honey-colored crusting, and no punctate erosions. A skin swab sent by her primary care doctor last week grew only normal skin flora.

My impression is a moderate flare of atopic dermatitis without signs of secondary infection, along with stable seasonal allergic rhinitis. I explained that her swab result means she does not need an antibiotic.

I am stopping the hydrocortisone 1% cream because it is too weak for these plaques. I am starting triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily to the elbows and knees for up to two weeks, and hydrocortisone 2.5% ointment twice daily to the neck for up to one week. She will continue cetirizine 10 mg daily and apply a fragrance-free petrolatum-based moisturizer twice daily and after bathing. I reviewed safe steroid use, short lukewarm showers, and avoiding wool and fragranced products, and I gave her written instructions so she can review the answers at home. If control is inadequate, we will discuss a biologic treatment option. Follow-up in four weeks.
